summary: Describes version 4 minor version 1 of the Network File System protocol, including features retained from the base NFSv4 protocol and later extensions. The minor version does not depend on minor version 0 and is considered a separate protocol. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS lets one computer use files stored on another computer as if they were local. This document describes version 4.1 of NFS, where every request runs inside a session so a retry is not done twice, where the client can be given the job of looking after a file while nobody else wants it, and where the client can read and write file data straight to storage devices in parallel.

questions: how does nfs version 4 minor version 1 work
subtitle: The version of NFS built around sessions, delegations and parallel data access, with a rewritten account of moving file systems between servers.

tldr.problem: Earlier NFS versions could not run a request exactly once, could not send callbacks back to a client through a firewall, and had no way to read and write file data in parallel across several servers. The earlier version 4.1 document also left two features half described: using several connections at once, and moving a file system between servers.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4.1 puts every request inside a session, gives each session a bounded set of slots so a retried request is executed only once, folds locking, delegations and parallel data access into one protocol, and adds attributes that tell a client where a file system now lives.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8881 obsoletes RFC 5661 as the specification of NFSv4.1, with a limited-scope rewrite aimed at trunking and Transparent State Migration. The document's own appendices list security, internationalization and the versioning rules as work still to do.

facts.label: Slot sequence ID
facts.value: 32 bits; first use is 1, then wraps to 0 after 0xFFFFFFFF

today: RFC 8881 is a Proposed Standard from August 2020 that obsoletes RFC 5661, so it is the current specification of NFSv4.1. The updates that RFC 8434 and RFC 8178 apply to RFC 5661 also apply to this document, and its own appendices list the treatment of security, internationalization and the versioning rules as work that a later revision still has to do.

sections.title: Why This Update Exists
sections.content:
RFC 8881 describes version 4 minor version 1 of the Network File System (NFS) protocol, the second minor version of NFSv4. It keeps the goals of NFSv4: improved access and good performance on the Internet, strong security with negotiation built into the protocol, good cross-platform interoperability, and a framework for protocol extensions. It adds goals of its own: to correct significant structural weaknesses found in the base protocol, to add specific features based on experience with it, and to support clustered servers with scalable parallel access to files.

The document is a limited-scope update of RFC 5661, which it obsoletes. Two features defined for minor version 0 had never been fully addressed in minor version 1: trunking, the simultaneous use of several connections between a client and server, and Transparent State Migration, which transfers a file system between servers while the client keeps its locking state. Most of the work is a rewritten Section 11 on the multi-server namespace. Appendix A explains why the changes were needed, and Appendix B lists what changed.

NFSv4.1 has no dependency on NFSv4.0 and is treated as a separate protocol. Compared with NFSv4.0 the main differences are the sessions model, parallel access to data through pNFS, the RECLAIM_COMPLETE operation, delegations on directories as well as on regular files, attributes that can be set atomically during an exclusive create, preservation of open files that are removed, better compatibility with Microsoft Windows access control lists, data retention, and identification of the implementation.

The document also lists the work it deliberately leaves for a later revision: agreement with the NFSv4-wide versioning rules of RFC 8178, the requirements for pNFS layout types in RFC 8434, many deferred errata reports, a new approach to internationalization, and a revised treatment of security.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is the current rulebook for NFS version 4.1, the second minor version of the file sharing protocol. It updates the earlier version 4.1 document mainly to describe two things properly: using several network connections at once, and moving a file system to another server while the client keeps its locks.

sections.title: Requests, Client IDs and Version Rules
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 is a Remote Procedure Call (RPC) application that uses RPC version 2 and the eXternal Data Representation (XDR). Unlike NFSv3, which used separate protocols for locking, network status and mounting, every minor version of NFSv4 uses a single RPC protocol, and the facilities that used to be separate protocols are folded into it.

There are exactly two RPC procedures, NULL and COMPOUND. A COMPOUND carries a series of operations that the server evaluates in order, without any atomicity guarantee. When one operation returns a failing result, evaluation ends and the results so far go back to the client. Chaining several LOOKUP operations resolves a path with several components in one request, and combining OPEN with READ does the same work in a single round trip. Callbacks use the same shape, with the two callback procedures CB_NULL and CB_COMPOUND.

Each client instance is represented by a client ID, a 64-bit identifier the server assigns. The client identifies itself with a client owner: a 64-bit verifier that changes on every restart, plus an opaque owner string that stays the same across restarts of the same client. A client establishes and confirms its client ID by sending EXCHANGE_ID and then CREATE_SESSION with the returned client ID. Until that is done, the only operations a client may send are the ones needed to establish the client ID.

A server identifies itself with a server owner, a major identifier and a minor identifier, returned in the EXCHANGE_ID result. Matching major identifiers mean the two connections reach the same server, and matching minor identifiers mean a session can be shared across both connections. The client also receives a server scope, an opaque string that lets a group of servers tell clients that they have arranged never to give the same value to two different objects.

Because a server may offer several security mechanisms, the client can ask which ones apply to a given part of the namespace with the SECINFO and SECINFO_NO_NAME operations. A server that wants a different mechanism from the one in use returns NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC, and the client then chooses one the server allows.

Minor versions add rules so that the protocol can grow. Procedures are never added or deleted, minor versions may add operations to COMPOUND and CB_COMPOUND and may append attributes, and the structure of an existing operation or attribute is never changed. NFSv4.1 breaks two of the older guidelines: the sessions model and RECLAIM_COMPLETE are infrastructural, so they are REQUIRED rather than optional.

The transport must deliver data reliably and in order. Support for TCP is REQUIRED, and UDP on its own MUST NOT be used as an NFSv4.1 transport. The registered port for NFS over TCP is 2049.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything a client sends is one message holding a list of operations, and the server works through that list in order until one of them fails. The client also gets a number from the server that identifies it, and a standing arrangement, called a session, that ties its requests, its locks and its callbacks to that number.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Trunking
sections.content:
Clients and servers MUST support and MUST use the session feature. A session is a long-lived server object, created by a client and used over time from one or more transport connections. Its function is to hold the server's state about a client instance, and that state exists whether or not a connection exists. A client may create several sessions, but a single session MUST NOT serve multiple clients.

Each session has a fore channel for ordinary requests from the client to the server and, optionally, a backchannel for callbacks from the server to the client. The client creates the connections that carry the backchannel, which is what allows callbacks to pass through firewalls. NFSv4.1 servers MUST support backchannels. Each channel has its own reply cache.

State is tied to the client ID, not to any one session. State-changing operations may travel over different sessions that share the same client ID, and a callback may arrive over a session other than the one that obtained the state. The SEQUENCE operation says which session the rest of the request belongs to, and it MUST be the first operation of any session-enabled COMPOUND. Its main job is to carry the session identifier.

Trunking is the use of multiple connections between a client and a server in order to increase the speed of data transfer, and NFSv4.1 defines two forms of it. Session trunking associates several connections with one session. Client ID trunking associates several sessions with one client ID, so that locking state is shared across them. Servers MUST support both forms for a single network address, and MUST support client ID trunking for two target network addresses whenever they allow session trunking for those addresses.

The client decides which form applies by comparing the results of EXCHANGE_ID sent over the different connections. Session trunking is permitted when the client ID, the server owner major and minor identifiers and the server scope all match. Client ID trunking is permitted when the client ID, the major identifier and the server scope match. The client can verify these claims with RPCSEC_GSS or with the SSV mechanism described in Section 2.10.9.

The owner string the client sends should be unique, the same across restarts of the same client, and the same for every server network address the client uses, so that trunking works. The RFC warns against an approach that assumes the client's network address will not change, because addresses get reassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is a long-lived record that the server keeps for one client. It survives a broken connection, it carries the callbacks the server sends back, and it lets the client use several connections at once to move data faster.

sections.title: Exactly Once Semantics and the Reply Cache
sections.content:
Through the session, NFSv4.1 offers exactly once semantics (EOS) on both channels. Any COMPOUND or CB_COMPOUND that starts with SEQUENCE or CB_SEQUENCE MUST be executed by the receiver exactly once. The rule covers every request, not only the ones that change state. A repeated RENAME would fail the second time and report the wrong answer. A repeated WRITE is idempotent on its own, but if the first copy is still waiting in the server's internal I/O system while the retry is answered, a later overlapping write can be overwritten and the file corrupted. To keep implementations simple, the replier MUST enforce EOS for all requests.

The mechanism replaces the RPC transaction ID as the key of the duplicate request cache. The requester picks a slot ID in the range 0..N, where N starts out as ca_maxrequests - 1 and can be adjusted by the server. A slot holds a 32-bit sequence ID and the reply cached for it. The first time a slot is used, the requester MUST specify a sequence ID of one, and each reuse MUST specify one greater than the previous value, wrapping to zero after 0xFFFFFFFF.

The replier compares the received sequence ID with the one recorded in the slot. One greater means a new request, which is executed and the slot's sequence ID is increased. Equal means a retransmission, and the cached reply is returned. A lower value, or a value two or more greater, MUST get NFS4ERR_SEQ_MISORDERED. Because the number of slots is bounded, the slot-based reply cache cannot be overflowed, and the replier does not need to keep the request itself, only the reply.

The SEQUENCE operation also carries a highest_slotid, which lets the requester hand back unused slots and lets the replier raise or lower the limits it enforces. If the replier lowers the enforced limit and the requester keeps sending a higher one, the server MAY reply with NFS4ERR_BAD_HIGH_SLOT. A request larger than the negotiated maximum request size gets NFS4ERR_REQ_TOO_BIG, and a reply larger than the negotiated maximum reply size gets NFS4ERR_REP_TOO_BIG.

True and complete EOS across a server restart needs the reply cache in stable storage. A replier that agreed to persist a session MUST persist the session ID and the slot table with its sequence IDs and cached replies. After a restart, a retried request returns its cached result, while a new request gets NFS4ERR_DEADSESSION, which marks the session as dead.

Because each request is identified by the triple of session ID, slot ID and sequence ID, the server can also resolve a race between a callback and the reply to the request that caused it. The callback carries the referring triple in its CB_SEQUENCE, and the client can see that the request is still outstanding and act accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request that starts with SEQUENCE is run exactly once, even if the client sends it again because a connection broke. The server recognises the repeat by the slot and the sequence number the request carries, and it answers from a saved copy of the first reply instead of doing the work twice.

sections.title: Stateids, Leases and Crash Recovery
sections.content:
Locking is built into NFSv4.1, so the protocol is stateful. The server owns the state, the client requests changes, and every piece of state is named by a 128-bit stateid. A stateid has a 96-bit other field that identifies a set of locks and a 32-bit seqid that the server increments whenever that set changes. A new stateid starts with seqid one. A client may send seqid zero to mean the most current value, or a non-zero value, in which case the server returns NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID if it is too low and NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID if it is too high.

A stateid can stand for an open file, a set of byte-range locks, a file delegation, a directory delegation or a layout. Four special values are reserved. An all-zero other and seqid is the anonymous stateid, used in READ, WRITE and SETATTR to indicate the absence of any open state. An all-ones value is the READ bypass stateid, which the server MAY use to grant a read that would otherwise be denied. An other of zero with seqid one is the current stateid, whatever the last stateid returned by an operation in the same COMPOUND. An other of zero with seqid NFS4_UINT32_MAX is reserved as invalid.

All of the state a client holds shares one lease. A successful SEQUENCE on an unexpired lease renews it for the period given by the lease_time attribute, so a COMPOUND with nothing but a SEQUENCE is enough to stay alive. The sr_status_flags result tells the client about backchannel problems, revoked state and the need to reclaim state after a restart.

After a server restart the client must be able to get its locks back without another client being granted a conflicting lock. The server therefore opens a grace period, during which only reclaim-type requests are allowed and other requests get NFS4ERR_GRACE. Once the client has reclaimed what it holds, it sends RECLAIM_COMPLETE with rca_one_fs set to FALSE. A server MAY end the grace period before every client has sent it, but SHOULD NOT end it before a time equal to the lease period, so that clients have a chance to notice the restart. The RFC describes two edge conditions in which a client could reclaim a lock it had already lost; the server must either detect them and refuse with NFS4ERR_NO_GRACE, or record enough state in stable storage to detect them.

A short lease makes recovery fast but costs more renewal traffic, and a long lease does the opposite. Lease times are granted as a time delta, so the client and the server do not need synchronized clocks, but the client should subtract the propagation delay from the lease it is given.
sections.plainLanguage: Every lock, open and delegation the server holds for a client is named by a 128-bit number, and a second number inside it counts the changes to that set. The server renews the client's hold on all of its state each time a request arrives, and after a restart it gives clients a short window to ask for their locks back before anyone else can take them.

sections.title: Opens, Byte-Range Locks and Share Reservations
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 replaces the older way of opening a file with a single OPEN operation that can look up, create and lock at the same time, because share semantics cannot be implemented correctly with a separate share or unshare step. The client states the access it wants, READ, WRITE or BOTH, and the access it denies to others, and the server checks both against the current state of the file. The OPEN operation with the CREATE flag also replaces the older CREATE operation for regular files, so a create with a share can be done atomically.

A share reservation is established by OPEN and is mandatory: when the OPEN denies reading or writing, later READ and WRITE operations are rejected with NFS4ERR_LOCKED. A byte-range lock covers a range of bytes within a file and is created with the LOCK operation, which also names the owner of the lock. The owner is a state-owner value such as a thread or process ID, and it is combined with the client ID to identify the holder.

The server may treat byte-range locks as advisory or mandatory, or may decide per file, and in Windows environments they are always mandatory. The LOCK operation itself does not distinguish the two; the difference appears when the server handles a READ or WRITE. Each of those operations carries a stateid, and the stateid says what the client holds, an open, a set of byte-range locks or a delegation. If a conflicting share reservation or a mandatory byte-range lock is in the way, the server MUST refuse the operation.

Two special stateids change that check. The READ bypass stateid asks the server to bypass the locking checks for a read, and the server MAY grant access that would normally be denied. The same value in a WRITE or SETATTR is treated as the anonymous stateid, so a write never bypasses the check.

Clients can ask for a lock that waits. The READW_LT and WRITEW_LT lock types ask the server to deny the request now and notify the client later with a callback when the lock becomes available. Because that callback is OPTIONAL, clients must keep polling. To keep the polling fair, the server maintains an ordered list of pending blocking locks and may wait for a period equal to the lease time for the first waiting client to ask again.

A second OPEN for a file that the same open-owner already has upgrades the open: the access and deny bits are combined into one open, and the seqid of the stateid is incremented. Because OPENs for one owner may run in parallel, CLOSE and OPEN_DOWNGRADE should generally carry a non-zero seqid so that an upgrade is not lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a file in this version also states what the client wants to read or write and what it will not let another client do. The server checks those two lists against the state it holds for the file, and refuses the open when they conflict.

sections.title: Delegations and Client-Side Caching
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 does not provide distributed cache coherence. Instead it defines a more limited set of caching guarantees, so that locks and share reservations are not undermined by client caches, and it adds delegation. A delegation is a promise by the server that other clients will not touch the file in a conflicting way for as long as the delegation is held. Delegations are leased, recallable and revocable, like the other locks. Because the granting of a delegation is always conditional on the absence of conflicting access, clients MUST NOT assume that one will be granted.

When another client makes a conflicting request, the server recalls the delegation with a callback. The client flushes its modified state to the server and returns the delegation, and only then does the server decide the conflicting request. If the client does not answer, the server revokes the delegation. The server is free to recall a delegation whenever it judges that desirable, and changes made outside the protocol must also lead to a recall when they would invalidate the guarantees the delegation gives.

There are two types of open delegation. OPEN_DELEGATE_READ assures the client that the contents, the attributes except time_access, and the names of links to the file will not change without its knowledge; several read delegations may exist at once. OPEN_DELEGATE_WRITE lets the client handle all opens itself and modify the file data locally; only one may exist for a given file, and it is inconsistent with any read delegation. A write delegation lets the client change only the attributes intimately connected with the data, which are size, change, time_access, time_metadata and time_modify.

NFSv4.1 adds directory delegations, an OPTIONAL feature requested with GET_DIR_DELEGATION. They are read-only and cover the directory attributes and all entries in the directory. A client may also ask for asynchronous notifications of changes, so that a delegation need not be recalled for every change. No provision is made for reclaiming directory delegations after a client or server restart; the client simply asks again.

Without a delegation, cached data must be revalidated after an OPEN by comparing the change attribute with the cached value, and modified data must be flushed to the server before a file opened for writing is closed. With byte-range locks the same rules apply per range: the data in a newly locked range must be revalidated, and the modified data must be flushed and written to stable storage before the lock is released.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can let a client look after a file by itself for a while, as long as nobody else is using it. When somebody else wants the file, the server asks the client to hand it back before it decides what to do with the new request.

sections.title: Multi-Server Namespace, Trunking and Migration
sections.content:
Section 11 is the heart of this update. NFSv4.1 lets one namespace span several servers. The fs_locations and fs_locations_info attributes give the client the places where a file system can be found, with fs_locations_info preferred because it carries more detail, such as priority for use and whether the copy is writable. A file system can be present or absent at a position in a server's namespace. An absent file system contains nothing but its root, and any operation on it other than fetching location attributes returns NFS4ERR_MOVED. Absent file systems enable referrals, where one server directs the client to a file system provided by another. Use of multi-server namespaces is OPTIONAL.

The location attributes also drive trunking. The RFC separates trunking detection, deciding whether two network addresses are connected to the same server, from trunking discovery, the process by which a client obtains other addresses for that server. RFC 5661 defined the first but gave no description of the second, which is one of the gaps this document closes.

Two network addresses connected to the same server are server-trunkable and support client ID trunking. Two such addresses that can be used for one common session are session-trunkable. The RFC separates two network paths to one file system instance, where locking state is shared, from two replicas of a file system, where locking state is not shared, and it says plainly that RFC 5661 treated the second case as if it were the first.

When access moves between replicas, the client needs to be sure that the actions its locks forbid did not happen during the move. Two mechanisms give that assurance. The first is a per-file-system grace period on the destination server, during which the transferred client's locks are not contradicted. The second is Transparent State Migration, in which the locking state, and where possible the session state, are handed to the destination server. Transparent State Migration gives the smoother experience, because the client does not have to go through a reclaim process, but it needs a greater degree of coordination between the servers. The two are not mutually exclusive, and a server may well provide both. The protocol does not specify how a file system is moved between servers.

The client learns that a transition has happened when a request returns NFS4ERR_MOVED. It then fetches the location attributes, with integrity protection, and continues against the new server. When locking state has moved with the file system, the server sets the status bit SEQ4_STATUS_LEASE_MOVED in the SEQUENCE result, so that the client renews its lease on the new server.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can be told that the file system it is using now lives on a different server, and the RFC explains how the client keeps its locks and its session across that change. It also explains how the client learns about other addresses for the same server, so it can send data over several connections at once.

sections.title: Parallel NFS and the File Layout Type
sections.content:
Parallel NFS (pNFS) is an OPTIONAL feature that lets clients access the storage devices holding file data directly, and do so in parallel. It splits the work in two. A metadata server handles names, attributes and permissions. One or more storage devices hold the file data and are reached through a storage protocol, which can be NFSv4.1 itself, a block or volume protocol such as iSCSI, or an object protocol. A control protocol between the metadata server and the storage devices is outside the scope of this document. A pNFS server MUST still support ordinary NFSv4.1 access to any file it offers through pNFS.

The client asks for a layout with LAYOUTGET. A layout maps a byte range of a file to storage devices, belongs to a layout type, and is leased, recallable and revocable in the same way as a delegation. Layouts name devices by device ID, and GETDEVICEINFO resolves a device ID to an address. A client MUST hold a layout to send input or output to a storage device, and the storage device SHOULD reject input or output for a range the client holds no layout for. The other operations are LAYOUTCOMMIT, which tells the metadata server that data has been written and is ready to be committed, LAYOUTRETURN, and the callback CB_LAYOUTRECALL. Access rights still come from OPEN, LOCK and ACCESS.

Section 13 defines the file layout type LAYOUT4_NFSV4_1_FILES, which uses NFSv4.1 data servers. Data is divided into stripe units spread over the data servers in a repeating pattern. The stripe unit number for a file offset is the offset relative to nfl_pattern_offset, divided by the stripe unit size and rounded down. The minimum stripe unit size is 64 bytes. A client may send only the session management operations, plus COMMIT, READ, WRITE and PUTFH, to a data server, and it must use the filehandle the layout specifies.

The layout tells the client which data server each stripe unit goes to. In the example in Section 13.4.2, seven data servers are arranged in three groups and the striping index array has four entries, so the destinations of the stripe units repeat every four units. The client picks one address from the group and sends the read or write with the filehandle the layout gives it.

When a layout is revoked, the pNFS server MUST fence the client from the affected file on all of the data servers, so that no input or output continues for a layout that no longer exists. Before the metadata server hands out new layout state, it must make sure that the layout state of a previous instance is invalidated at the data servers, and it must not restripe a file until it has contacted all of those data servers.
sections.plainLanguage: With pNFS, the server keeps the names and permissions and the storage devices keep the file contents. The server tells the client which part of the file sits on which device, and the client reads and writes those parts itself, several at a time.

sections.title: Security Model and the Gaps the RFC Admits
sections.content:
Historically the authentication model of NFS was based on the entire machine being the NFS client, with the server trusting the client to authenticate the end user. NFSv4.1 implementations are REQUIRED to support a security model that uses end-to-end authentication, where an end user on a client mutually authenticates to a principal on the server. Clients and servers MUST implement RPCSEC_GSS and the Kerberos V5 mechanism, and both MUST support the authentication and integrity services; servers MUST support privacy and clients SHOULD. AUTH_SYS, which has no strong authentication, may also be implemented, but it is merely optional, so interoperability through it is not assured.

Integrity protection matters most for three operations. SECINFO and SECINFO_NO_NAME should be protected so that a man in the middle cannot push the client toward weaker algorithms. Fetching fs_locations and fs_locations_info should use integrity protection too, because an attacker could first force NFS4ERR_MOVED and then rewrite the locations to send the client to a server the attacker controls. The RFC advises that a client SHOULD NOT use unverified location entries as a basis for migration.

Sessions add a state protection problem, which Section 2.10.8.3 sets out. Without protection, an attacker who sends a SEQUENCE with a forged session ID and the slot ID the real client is about to use gets the server to answer the real client with the attacker's cached reply. An attacker who forges a client ID can create a session and release the real client's locks. The client chooses one of three protections when it creates its client ID: SP4_NONE, which waives protection, SP4_MACH_CRED, which uses a machine credential, and SP4_SSV, which uses a secret shared between the client and the server that both sides update with the SET_SSV operation.

Appendix C is candid about what is still missing. It says the Security Considerations section of this document was not thoroughly revised, so the earlier weaknesses stand. It lists the issues for a future revision: the continued use of AUTH_SYS, the lack of attention to pervasive monitoring attacks, where CREATE_SESSION without privacy protection exposes the session ID to view, and the lack of effective use of privacy and integrity even where the RPCSEC_GSS infrastructure is present. The authors add that a threat analysis would be likely to conclude that NFSv4.1 does not meet the goal of secure use on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients and servers must be able to prove to each other who they are, and the RFC says that the exchange between them should be protected as well. It also admits that the earlier text did not analyse the threats properly, and lists the problems that a later revision has to fix.

items.desc: Treated as anonymous in WRITE and SETATTR; in READ the server may grant access it would otherwise deny.

items.desc: Whatever the last stateid returned by an operation in the same COMPOUND.

items.label: Invalid stateid
items.desc: Reserved as invalid; the server must return NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID.
